function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents you’ll need to add to the repo.

> **⚠️**  
> *These commands assume you have `git`, `docker`, `kubectl`, and `node` installed on the machine you’re running them from.*  
> *If you’re on Windows, use PowerShell or WSL; on macOS/Linux the commands below work as‑is.*

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create the required artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# 2.1 Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image
FROM node:18-slim

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-slim` is small, stable, and contains everything you need.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** – adjust if your app uses a different port.*

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s/` and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
# 2.2 deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use another registry
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
# 2.2 service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80          # Service port
      targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **Tip:**  
> If you want external access, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` and expose the desired port.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` and add `ci.yml`:

```yaml
# 2.3 ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Node.js
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Cache npm dependencies
      - uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: ~/.npm
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-node-

      # Install dependencies
      - run: npm ci

      # Run tests (if any)
      - run: npm test || true

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker tag ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Push Docker image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Installs Node.js 18 and caches `npm`.  
> 3. Runs tests (if you have any).  
> 4. Builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA and `latest`.  
> 5. Logs into GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
> 6. Pushes both tags.

> **Prerequisites**  
> *Make sure the repo has the `GHCR` namespace (`zelarhq`) and that you have write access.*  
> *If you prefer Docker Hub, replace `ghcr.io/zelarhq/...` with your Docker Hub repo and use `docker/login-action` with your Docker Hub credentials.*

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
# 3. Add all new/changed files
git add Dockerfile k8s/ deployment.yaml service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# 4. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"

# 5. Push to main
git push origin main
```

---

## 4️⃣ Verify

After the push, you should see:

* A new **Actions** tab with a successful run.  
* The Docker image available in **GitHub Packages** (or Docker Hub if you switched).  
* The `k8s/` directory containing the deployment and service YAMLs.

You can now apply the K8s manifests to any cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| Artifact | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight container for the Node.js app |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys 2 replicas of the app |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Exposes the app inside the cluster |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Automates build & push on every push to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag, registry, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. Happy coding!
